name: Ghomala' (Bapa)
place: 2nd-degree chiefdom of Bapa, Bangou subdivision (Hauts-Plateaux, West)
overview: A people of the Hauts-Plateaux, the Bapa (Pepa) settled on a rugged site never occupied before them, rich in waterfalls, caves and sacred forests. A hereditary chiefdom linked to sister chiefdoms such as Batié, a cult of skulls and ancestors, and the great biennial kan festival, where young boys are initiated and shape their identity.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, in relationship with many neighbours (Batcham, Bana, Baleng…); most Bapa speak several languages.
The speech variety of Bapa is not spoken elsewhere in this form.
Formerly endogamous, the Bapa today marry both within and outside the group, men and women alike.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The rugged site was not occupied before them; waterfalls, caves and forests make it a veritable place of pilgrimage, which preserves the authenticity of the West.
The Bapa are said to have come from Batié (another version cites Haut-Nkam); the chiefdoms remain “sisters” and visit each other during major ceremonies.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: The chiefdoms of the Hauts-Plateaux are linked (politics, cults, festivals); society is hierarchical (chief, notables…).
Decisions originate at the base and rise by stages (neighbourhood, notables, council, chief), by vote and by consensus.
Anyone can meet the chief, regardless of sex or age.
Hereditary succession within the royal family, generally from father to son.
Roles passed down in families: marriage trainers, midwives, healers, specialists in skull removal, gravediggers.
In public, the wife shows great respect towards her husband; the chief is greeted with a bow.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the woman joins her husband's family.
The boy becomes a man when he can marry, between 20 and 30; the girl, when her body changes and she can run a household.
Steps: “knocking at the door”, engagement, bride price. The two families exchange gifts.
Kola (sharing and clarity, also used in divination), raffia wine (alliance of families and ancestors), palm oil, goats, kitchen utensils.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Cults of skulls, gods, ancestors and God, as among the other Bamiléké, especially in the dry season.
Natural sacred places that belong to no family: waterfalls, caves, rocks, sacred forests.
At birth, the priests of the community name the child and reveal their mission. Death is a family and community tragedy; the deceased remains linked to the living.
Taboos: incest, sitting on the chair of one's father's wife. Prohibitions: striking one's parents, stealing in sacred places, eating one's totem animal.
Serious offences: harming the chief's wife, witchcraft, murder, desecration of skulls; they led to expulsion.
Divination with or without a medium (foliage, animal parts, kola, cowries).

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Trade, construction, livestock rearing (goats, pigs, poultry), farming.
The land belongs to families and is passed on by inheritance; the heir receives all the possessions of the deceased.
Varied crafts: bamboo and rattan furniture, straw roofing, masks, drums and tam-tams, iron objects.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Dress expresses status: the quality of the cap, of the animal skin worn at ceremonies and of the mask; likewise among titled women.
Traditional medicine, rich in plants and specialists, remains very much alive.
Beauty refers to ethics: a pure and healthy life; inner beauty is sought in men as in women.
Courtship: propriety and kindness; for the woman, gentleness, self-sacrifice, calm, hard work, a sense of sharing and devotion.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms and dances: ndimasa, kan (kougan dance), sameli, ntchen; instruments: tam-tam, drum, whistle, balafon, beads.
Festival: the kan, every two years in the dry season, where young boys are initiated into the life of society.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The Bapa like to live in community and to share joys and sorrows; marriages, mutual help and development are settled in meetings. The group has managed to preserve its authenticity.

sections.title: The names
items: There are markers for men, women, twins and the child who follows them.
The name depends on the context of the birth, happy or unhappy.
One changes name at each ennoblement, on receiving new titles; the title precedes the name of nobles.
The founding chief was called Youdom.

lessons.title: Who are the Ghomala' (Bapa)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Ghomala' (Bapa) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition

vocabulary.frenchText: At the bottom of the tarot fields

lessons.competence: Introduce the Ghomala' (Bapa) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Ghomala' (Bapa) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Ghomala' (Bapa) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Ghomala' (Bapa) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Ghomala' (Bapa) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Majority group, in relation with many neighbours (Batcham, Bana, Baleng…); most Bapa speak several languages. • The speech variety of Bapa is not spoken elsewhere in this form. • Formerly endogamous, the Bapa today marry within and outside the group, men and women alike. • The site, rugged, was not occupied before them; waterfalls, caves and forests make it a true place of pilgrimage, which keeps the authenticity of the West. • The Bapa are said to have come from Batié (another version cites Haut-Nkam); the chiefdoms remain “sisters” and visit each other at major ceremonies.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: A people of the Hauts-Plateaux, the Bapa (Pepa) settled on a rugged site never occupied before them, rich in waterfalls, caves and sacred forests. A hereditary chiefdom linked to sister chiefdoms such as Batié, a cult of skulls and ancestors, and the great biennial kan festival, where young boys are initiated and shape their identity.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Ghomala' (Bapa) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)

objectives: Linking food to the living environment

lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Ghomala' (Bapa), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.

lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Ghomala' (Bapa), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Ghomala' (Bapa).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: nkui tubers, yellow sauce with cassava or maize flour. • Drinks: raffia wine. • Trade, construction, livestock rearing (goats, pigs, poultry), farming. • Land belongs to families and is passed on by inheritance; the heir receives all the property of the deceased.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Ghomala' (Bapa) mainly eat nkui tubers, yellow sauce with cassava or maize flour. Traditional drinks: raffia wine. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Ghomala' (Bapa)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Ghomala' (Bapa), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Ghomala' (Bapa). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Ghomala' (Bapa), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Ghomala' (Bapa). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Trade, building, livestock (goats, pigs, poultry), farming. • Land belongs to families and is passed on by inheritance; the heir receives all the property of the deceased. • Varied crafts: bamboo and rattan furniture, thatched roofs, masks, drums and tom-toms, iron objects.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Trade, construction, livestock rearing (goats, pigs, poultry), farming. Land belongs to families and is passed down by inheritance; the heir receives all the belongings of the deceased.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Ghomala' (Bapa)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Ghomala' (Bapa), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Ghomala' (Bapa). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Ghomala' (Bapa), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Ghomala' (Bapa). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Cults of skulls, gods, ancestors and God, as among the other Bamileke, especially in the dry season. • Natural sacred places that belong to no family: waterfalls, caves, rocks, sacred forests. • At birth, the priests of the community name the child and reveal their mission. Death is a family and community tragedy; the deceased remains bound to the living. • Taboos: incest, sitting on the chair of one's father's wife. Prohibitions: striking one's parents, stealing in sacred places, eating one's totem animal. • Serious offences: harming the chief's wife, witchcraft, murder, desecration of skulls; these led to expulsion.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cults of skulls, of the gods, of the ancestors and of God, as among the other Bamileke, especially in the dry season. Natural sacred places that belong to no family: waterfalls, caves, rocks, sacred forests.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Ghomala' (Bapa) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Ghomala'
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Ghomala' (Bapa) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Ghomala' (Bapa) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Ghomala' (Bapa) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Ghomala' (Bapa) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Ghomala'. • Greeting formulae: U yoge ntazè A ngèke = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); U liè = morning greeting (one person); Pu yogyele = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: tchu, pwe, Tan, kwe, Té/ yaté. • The founding chief was called Youdom. • The Bapa like living in community and sharing joys and sorrows; marriages, mutual aid and development are settled in meetings. The group has managed to preserve its authenticity.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Ghomala' are the first steps towards communicating with the Ghomala' (Bapa). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
